deep.reconstruction:
This page carries only a drawing, made in green, orange and dark-green felt pen with some pencil on the back of a CRAY2 JCL listing. There is no text by Grothendieck, so any reading of the mathematics is conjectural.

The neighbouring pages give the frame. The previous page works in the space of pseudo-lines (Δ, with a lifted or double-cover version Δ̃ and its boundary Δ̃_∞). It discusses specialisation D → D' of a pseudo-line D to a pseudo-line D' through a point s, and the two 'rives' (sides) of D'∖{s}. Its key claim is that the antipodal map gives a canonical combinatorial isomorphism between the two arcs of D̃' cut out by s̃ and s̃⁻. This yields a canonical isomorphism from 'the side of specialisations of D used' onto a combinatorial interval I(D', s).

The drawing shows five adjoining discs or ovals: two smaller ovals at upper left, one central disc, and two large discs at right and lower right. Each is crossed by many orange curves running from boundary to boundary and crossing pairwise. This is the standard disc model of the projective plane: the boundary circle is the line at infinity with antipodal points identified, and each pseudo-line is an arc joining two antipodal boundary points. Several orange curves run continuously from one disc into the next through the tangency points, notably from the left oval through the central disc and down into the lower-right disc. This suggests the discs are cells or charts glued together, or successive states of an arrangement under specialisation.

Dark-green arcs with arrowheads are traced along parts of the boundaries. One is labelled with small letters (read as p, q, p') at the top of the right disc; others sit near the junction of the central, right and lower-right discs, and one runs along the shared boundary of the central disc. These look like orientations of boundary arcs and identification or transport maps between them. That fits both themes: the antipodal identification of two boundary arcs (previous page) and gluing polygonal discs along edges by orientation-reversing affine maps fixed by transport isomorphisms φ_a (next page, where a surface is built from a combinatorial graph with polygonal structures, i.e. a ribbon graph / map).

A plausible reading is a heuristic picture of how local disc models of pseudo-line arrangements fit together. Arrangements are compared across adjacent cells via boundary arcs with matched or reversed orientations. This is a step toward describing the space (or a cell decomposition) of pseudo-line configurations, or the surface swept by specialisations, combinatorially. The pencil zigzag in the left oval and the wavy marks in the central disc look like trial sketches or hatching of a region (perhaps a 'side swept by the specialisation').
errors: No checkable mathematical statements on this page. The drawing is a heuristic sketch, and its exact meaning (what the five discs represent, what the labelled arrows identify) cannot be fixed from the image alone.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a purely pictorial page with no stated result. It documents Grothendieck's hands-on 1983–84 work on pseudo-line arrangements, linking it to his map/ribbon-graph gluing formalism. That link is of historical interest, but nothing on the page can be identified as a new result or a concrete missed connection.
transcription_corrections: Small dark-green labels at the top of the right disc read roughly 'p', 'q' (or 'J'), and 'p'' or '9'. The labels near the junction of the central, right and lower-right discs are tiny and illegible; one may be 'p' next to an arrowhead pointing into the junction.

The JCL listing is printed upside down on the back of the sheet. It includes 'XXCSSBATCH EXEC PGM=CRBATCH,REGION=&REG,PARM=&P', 'XXSTEPLIB DD DSN=CISI.PROD.CSSBATCH.V1.YY01,DISP=SHR', 'XXCRJIF DD DSN=SYS1.CR.JIF,DISP=SHR' and 'XXSYSIN DD DDNAME=CRAYIN'. It is printer stock, not Grothendieck's content.
The pencil marks in the upper-left oval and the wavy dark marks in the central disc are scribbles or hatching, not text.
